title: Graphene Josephson diodes from inherent asymmetric disorder
authors: Ivan Villani, Luca Chirolli, Matteo Carrega, Alessandro Crippa, Elia Strambini, Francesco Giazotto, Vaidotas Miseikis, Camilla Coletti, Fabio Beltram, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Stefan Heun, Sergio Pezzini
abstract: Josephson diodes are non-reciprocal superconducting devices characterized by different switching currents depending on the current flow direction. They recently attracted considerable theoretical and experimental attention, in view of their possible application as rectifying elements in the field of superconducting electronics, and as probes to investigate symmetry breaking mechanisms in mesoscopic systems. In this work, we show that graphene Josephson junctions provide rectification of supercurrent with an efficiency exceeding 20%. The effect appears applying a mT out-of-plane magnetic field and is enhanced close to the nodes of the Fraunhofer interference pattern. Our theoretical model identifies long-range scattering potentials in the junction as the symmetry-breaking mechanism, which yields supercurrent rectification in highly transparent junctions. While graphene stands as an ultra-clean transmission medium, our work shows that unavoidable residual disorder in a clean two-dimensional system is sufficient to promote this effect. Tailoring of the inversion (mirror) symmetry breaking could be obtained via proper design of external gates.
summary: The research reports on achieving significant supercurrent rectification in graphene Josephson junctions using inherent structural disorder. By combining low-temperature experiments with theoretical modeling, the authors prove that even minor, unavoidable disorder can induce diode behavior by breaking mirror symmetry. This work is vital for advancing superconducting electronics based on 2D materials.
main_problem: The study demonstrates that graphene Josephson junctions inherently exhibit supercurrent rectification (Josephson diode effect) due to asymmetric disorder, even in highly clean systems.
main_result: Supercurrent rectification efficiency exceeding 20% was achieved under an out-of-plane magnetic field, confirming that residual long-range disorder is sufficient to break the necessary mirror symmetry.
method: The work combines experimental measurements of V-I curves and Fraunhofer patterns with theoretical modeling based on a tight-binding Hamiltonian approach.
model_or_system: The physical system is an hBN-encapsulated graphene Josephson junction contacted by Niobium leads. The theory models the transport using a tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating disorder potentials $V(x, y)$ and magnetic field effects.
key_observables: Supercurrent rectification efficiency ($\eta$), switching currents ($I_{	ext{sw}+}, I_{	ext{sw}-}$), and Fraunhofer interference patterns modulated by current direction.
important_parameters: Out-of-plane magnetic field ($B$), backgate voltage ($V_{BG}$), and the strength/nature of the long-range scattering potential (disorder).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that residual disorder provides the necessary asymmetry to break mirror symmetry, and approximations like the Andreev limit are used in theoretical derivations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate device schematics, V-I curves showing directional switching currents at different magnetic fields, and Fraunhofer patterns demonstrating non-reciprocity.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the necessity of symmetry breaking (time-reversal + mirror) to presenting experimental evidence of high rectification efficiency, followed by theoretical modeling confirming that disorder is the source of this asymmetry.
why_interesting: This work provides a clean platform (graphene) for observing non-reciprocal quantum transport phenomena, which are crucial for developing superconducting electronic components and understanding symmetry breaking in mesoscopic superconductors.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Top view schematics of device layout. Graphene is encapsulated in hBN and edge-contacted by Nb leads. The heterostructure is placed on top of a Si/SiO2 substrate, which acts as a backgate via the application of a backgate voltage VBG. A current I is applied and flows through the junction, and the voltage drop is measured. Currents flowing in either positive (I+) or negative (I−) directions are indicated, respectively, in black and red. Magnetic field B is applied in the out-of-plane direction. Mirror symmetry axis Mx is indicated. (b) Voltage-current (V-I) curve at B = 0 showing switching-retrapping behaviour. Positive and negative flowing currents are represented respectively...

Figure 2: (a) Backgate sweep: sample resistance R as a function of backgate voltage VBG, measured by applying a large DC current bias. The acquisition position of the Fraunhofer patterns in b,d,f is indicated. T = 4.2 K, B = 0 T. (b-g) Upper row: Fraunhofer patterns (voltage drop |V | as function of out-of-plane magnetic field B and DC bias current Ibias). Lower row: corresponding rectification parameter η at different backgate voltage values. The relative position to the charge neutrality point ∆VBG = VBG −VCNP (VCNP = −3.6 V) is indicated at the top of each panel. (b-c) VBG = −20 V. (d-e) VBG = 0 V. (f-g) VBG = +20 V.

Figure 3: (a) Onsite potential V1(r) = V f1(r) for V = Vmax = 0.01 t. The spatial coordinates are in units of the lattice constant. (b) Calculated Fraunhofer patterns (I+ c and |I− c |) for V = Vmax and chemical potential µ = 0.3t. (c) Color-coded evolution of the rectification coefficient η for varying V in the range −Vmax < V < Vmax, as a function of applied magnetic flux 2eΦ/h. (d) Onsite potential V2(r) = V f2(r) for V = Vmax = 0.01 t. (e-f) Same as b,c, but for the onsite potential V2 shown in d.

Figure 4: (a) Onsite potential V1 for V = Vmax = 0.01 t. (b) Calculated Fraunhofer patterns (I+ c and |I− c |) for the case of armchair edges for µ = 0.3t. (c) Color-coded evolution of the rectification coefficient η with chemical potential µ, crossing the Dirac point. (d) Graphene strip with armachair edges. (e-f) Same as b-c, but for a graphene strip with zigzag as shown in g.
